Power is the average AC input of the whole server at 100% target load, measured by a SPEC-accepted power analyser (power-supply losses, fans, BMC, disks and network cards included); submissions are vendor-tuned (BIOS, JVM, often one DIMM per channel and one power supply), so deployed servers draw more. rows.bench: llama.cpp CUDA, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B 4-bit, continuous 1,024-token answers on battery (whole-laptop power read by Windows)
rows.note: Generation speed and power from the same run: Frandroid chained 30 answers of 1,024 tokens (about 7 minutes) on battery in Performance mode and read the whole laptop's draw, 89 to 93 W at 72 tok/s; the battery fell about 1.56% (of 99.9 Wh) a minute, which is 93.5 W, and the review gives 0.36 Wh per 1,000 tokens (0.77 tokens per joule). Weaker: the power is the battery side, read by Windows, with the internal display on, not a wall meter with an external monitor as for Notebookcheck's readings; it leaves out the charger's losses, so the power range runs from 89 W to 10% above the 93.5 W drain figure (102.9 W), what a wall reading could add. Plugged in, the same run held 75.2 to 76.8 tok/s with the GPU part at 43.8 W against 30.3 W on battery, so a plugged-in point would draw more. The N1X (RTX Spark) is a Windows-on-Arm laptop SoC with 20 Arm cores and a 6,144-core Blackwell GPU sharing 128 GB of LPDDR5X (about 273 to 300 GB/s), the GB10's design in a 45 to 80 W laptop envelope; no GB10 (DGX Spark) figure is used here.

est.bench: Cinebench 2024 (speed of the MacBook Pro 16)
est.note: Speed borrowed from the 16-inch: Cinebench 2024 all-core as measured by Notebookcheck on the MacBook Pro 16 with M4 Max (2069 points). Power estimated: the 16-inch drew 92.2 W at the wall in the Cinebench 2024 all-core run (87.1 to 105.4 W), within the 14-inch's 96 W adapter, so it is kept as the central value; the range runs from 78.4 W (0.85 times, for a 14-inch that throttles to a lower sustained power) up to the 16-inch's 105.4 W peak, which is above what the adapter delivers. No wall measurement exists for the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M4 Max: speed and power here are estimates, not readings of this machine. Speed is borrowed from the 16-inch (16-core CPU, 40-core GPU, the same configuration the 14-inch offers at the top); the 14-inch has a smaller cooler and a 96 W adapter, so its sustained multi-core and GPU speed is likely a bit lower, but no source found measures by how much, so the speed is not scaled. Apple's own figures for this machine are the ENERGY STAR record (A3185), shown with the point.

est.bench: Ollama (LMSYS) gpt-oss 20B MXFP4
est.note: Generation speed measured: Ollama, MXFP4, as tested by LMSYS; the same model under llama.cpp runs about 1.7 times faster on GB10 (82.7 to 88 tokens per second), so the engine matters as much as the chip. No wall power was measured with these runs. Power is estimated at 160 W, the wall reading Tom's Hardware gives for the DGX Spark under a mainly GPU-driven load and Notebookcheck for the HP ZGX Nano G1n (the same GB10 hardware) in sustained LLM inference; the range runs from 120 W (just below the 122.8 to 156 W peaks Jeff Geerling metered on the Dell Pro Max with GB10 across models) to 206 W (Notebookcheck's maximum). Geerling's peaks sit below 160 W, so these points more likely understate the efficiency than overstate it. The Spark idles at 35 to 45 W, so short runs fare worse than long ones.

Submissions mix oMLX versions, macOS versions, memory sizes and chassis (oMLX does not record whether it is a MacBook or a desktop), so a bin can sit 10 to 20% off another; runs implausibly fast for the chip's memory bandwidth (speculative decoding) were dropped before the median. No power was measured: wall power is this chip's Llama 2 7B decode-power estimate (48 W, 28.6 to 83 W), widened by 10%, as for the small oMLX sets. A dense 12 to 32B model streams two to four times the bytes per token of the 7B model while staying memory-bound, so the draw should be close to the 7B run's, if anything a little higher. Only a 16-core GPU bin is used for this chip, while the power estimate is for the 19-core GPU, so the power may be a little high.

This is a mixture of experts that reads only its active experts per token (about 3B active). Submissions mix oMLX versions, macOS versions, memory sizes and chassis (oMLX does not record whether it is a MacBook or a desktop), so a bin can sit 10 to 20% off another; runs implausibly fast for the chip's memory bandwidth (speculative decoding) were dropped before the median. No power was measured: wall power is this chip's Llama 2 7B decode-power estimate (23 W, 13.5 to 39.1 W), widened by 10%, as for the small oMLX sets. Only the active experts are read per token, so the memory system may be less busy than with the 7B model and the efficiency here is more likely understated than overstated.
